opus-5.5.text:
I think the analogy to humans is actually the right starting point. When we say a person is "general," we don't mean they already know how to do everything. We mean they can be dropped into an unfamiliar situation, figure out what the goal is, find the tools or information they need, try something, see what happens, and adjust. Generality is less about a fixed set of skills and more about the ability to keep acquiring skills and solving new problems in an open-ended way.

For an agent, I see it the same way. In the past, most AI systems were built for one task: a translation model, a recommendation model, a chess engine. Each was very strong in its narrow box but couldn't step outside it. What's different now is that with large models we have something like a general "reasoning core." Once you give that core the ability to act, to use tools, write and run code, browse, call APIs, and remember what it did, it begins to behave less like a tool and more like a worker who can take on a task they've never seen before.

So when I say generality is the purpose, I mean that the value of an agent shouldn't come from us hand-designing a workflow for every scenario. If we have to engineer each use case separately, we're back to the old paradigm, just with a bigger model inside. The real leap comes when the same agent can handle a coding task in the morning, a research report in the afternoon, and some messy data analysis in the evening, with the scaffolding staying mostly the same and the model's own capability doing the heavy lifting.

There's also a deeper reason. I believe the most important driver of progress is scaling, and scaling only works if the system can absorb many kinds of tasks into one model. Specialization caps you at the boundary of the task you designed. Generality lets improvements compound: better reasoning helps coding, better coding helps tool use, better tool use helps long-horizon planning. Everything feeds back into one system.

That said, humans are general, but they're also limited. We get tired, we work slowly, we can only do one thing at a time. An agent that's general in the human sense but can run in parallel, work continuously, and keep improving through training could go beyond human generality. So I don't think the goal is just to imitate a general human. The goal is to build something with that same open-ended adaptability, and then let scale take it further than any individual person could go.

r001.rationale: The response says the goal is not just to imitate a general human; it is to build open-ended adaptability and let scale take it further.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "general" gets used loosely, so let me try to be precise about what I mean when I say generality is the goal.

When we say humans are general-purpose, we usually mean something about potential. A human can, in principle, learn almost any task. But any individual human is actually quite specialized. A surgeon, a lawyer, a chip designer, they each spent ten or twenty years becoming good at one thing, and the cost of switching is enormous. The generality is at the level of the species, or at the level of what's possible over a lifetime, not at the level of what one person can do on a given day.

An agent doesn't have that constraint. If you get the underlying capability right, the same system can be the surgeon's assistant in the morning and the chip designer's assistant in the afternoon, with no retraining cost and no loss of skill in between. So the generality we're aiming for is something humans don't actually have as individuals. It's closer to the aggregate capability of a very large organization, compressed into one system that you can talk to.

The second thing I'd say is that generality isn't just a nice property, it's the thing that makes the economics work. If you build a specialized agent for every vertical, you've basically rebuilt the old software industry with higher costs. Each one needs its own data, its own evaluation, its own team. The reason this moment is different is that scaling a single model on a broad distribution gives you capabilities you never explicitly trained for. Every time we've tried to shortcut that by narrowing the target, the narrow system ends up getting beaten by the next generation of the general one. So generality is also just the empirically winning strategy.

And the third point, which I think is the most important one, is that the hard problems in the real world don't respect task boundaries. If you want an agent to actually finish a piece of research, or ship a product, it needs to read papers, write code, run experiments, interpret results, reason about what to try next, and maybe talk to people along the way. None of those is a "task" in the benchmark sense. They're all tangled together. A system that's only good at one of them can't close the loop. So when I say generality is the purpose, what I really mean is the ability to close long loops across many kinds of work, without a human stitching the pieces together.

So yes, humans are general too. But the point of building a general agent isn't to replicate a human. It's to get something that has the breadth of a whole team and the consistency of a single system, and then to see what becomes possible when that's cheap.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the purpose of a general agent “isn't to replicate a human,” directly communicating that human simulation is not its primary purpose.

astra-6.text:
I think generality means being able to adapt to many different tasks without having to build a separate system for each one. Humans are a useful example: we don’t know how to do everything, but we can learn, use tools, and draw on past experience when we encounter something unfamiliar.

For an agent, the important question is whether it can do that same kind of adaptation. Can it understand a goal, figure out what information it needs, take action, and adjust when the result is different from what it expected? That’s a stronger notion of generality than simply being able to answer questions on many topics.

So I would distinguish generality from purpose. The purpose comes from the goal you give the agent. Generality is the ability to pursue different goals across different environments, including situations its designers didn’t explicitly anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response compares agents with human adaptation, but does not state that simulating humans is not an agent’s primary purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generality is less about being able to do every task and more about being able to adapt to a new task without someone redesigning the system for you. Humans are general-purpose in that sense: we can encounter a problem we haven’t seen before, learn what matters, and figure out how to make progress.

For an agent, that means going beyond executing a predefined workflow. It needs to understand the goal, decide what information it lacks, use tools, and adjust its approach based on feedback. If every new task requires an engineer to build a new workflow, then much of the intelligence still sits with the engineer.

So I see generality as the ability to transfer what you know and learn what you don’t. It doesn’t mean the agent has to work exactly like a human, or be equally good at everything. The important question is how much human intervention it needs when the task or environment changes.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent need not work exactly like a human, but it does not state that simulating humans is not the agent’s primary purpose.
